Session plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Teachers leave with a second lens for the student whose behavior keeps repeating (a skill that isn't there yet, rather than a will that's missing), five moves for the heated moment, three steps for the talk afterward, and one two-minute habit that heads off trouble before it starts.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per teacher
  • The faculty quick reference (last slide), printed or linked
  • Board space for two columns: want to / can

Flow

  1. 5 minOpening: a student whose behavior wore you down (private cards)
  2. 5 minTwo lenses: want to, or can?
  3. 6 minThe research on understanding first
  4. 6 minWhat's getting in the way: skills and problems
  5. 5 minIn the moment: calm first, talk later
  6. 6 minTalk later: three steps (practice in pairs)
  7. 4 minThe first two minutes
  8. 5 minThree students (small groups)
  9. 3 minOne student, two weeks

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Thirty minutes: the opening card (3), two lenses (4), the research (4), what's getting in the way (4), in the moment (4), talk later with one pair practice (5), the first two minutes (3), one student, two weeks (3). Share the faculty quick reference afterward.

Before you present
Two presenters, one voice.

A natural split: the counselor or psychologist presents the two lenses, the research and the heated moment; learning support presents the lagging skills, the talk-later steps and how they fit with learning plans.

Nobody here is doing it wrong.

Clear limits and consequences help most students, and every teacher in the room uses them. Say so. This talk is for the few students those tools haven't reached.

Expectations stay.

Kids do well if they can doesn't mean anything goes. The expectation stays; what changes is how you help a student meet it. Safety always comes first.

Be clear about learning plans.

Accommodations written into a student's learning plan stay exactly as written. Many lagging skills are already named there, so check it first.

Ross Greene, in his words.

Present Collaborative and Proactive Solutions as his model and "kids do well if they can" as his line. His nonprofit, Lives in the Balance, has free tools for teachers who want more.

Teachers get worn down too.

A student who pushes every day takes a toll. Name that early and warmly. Nobody does their best problem solving while they're flooded, adults included.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Who gets read as defiant.

Teachers read a second misbehavior as a pattern faster when the student is Black, and Black students are suspended at higher rates. Slow down at the second incident and ask what's getting in the way.

Culture and respect.

Eye contact, volume, interrupting and arguing back mean different things in different homes. What reads as disrespect may be normal, even respectful, where a student comes from. Ask before you label it.

Neurodivergent students.

For students with ADHD, autism or a language disorder, the lagging skill is often part of the diagnosis. Check the learning plan and talk with learning support before you treat it as a choice.

What's happening at home.

Hunger, no sleep, a family crisis, housing or immigration worries can all show up as behavior. Ask privately, and bring what you learn to the counseling team.

Language.

A student learning English may act out when they're lost and can't say so. Check whether they understood the directions before you treat it as defiance.

Students being targeted.

An outburst can be a response to teasing you didn't see, including about race, sexuality or gender identity. Ask what happened right before.

What the research says

Ross Greene's model holds that kids do well if they can: challenging behavior shows up when the demands on a student outpace their skills. Adults find the lagging skills and unsolved problems, then solve the problems with the student.

Greene, Lost at School, 2008 (revised 2014); Greene, The Explosive Child

In a trial with 134 children ages 7 to 14 with oppositional defiant disorder, Collaborative and Proactive Solutions and parent management training both did better than a waitlist, with similar results.

Ollendick et al., Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 2016

In five middle schools, math teachers who did a short online exercise on empathic discipline (understanding the student's side and keeping the relationship) cut their students' suspension rate in half over the year, from 9.6% to 4.8%.

Okonofua, Paunesku and Walton, PNAS, 2016

Teachers who read about a student's second misbehavior were more troubled, and more likely to see the student as a troublemaker, when the student had a stereotypically Black name.

Okonofua and Eberhardt, Psychological Science, 2015

Putting feelings into words lowered activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm, when people looked at emotional images.

Lieberman et al., Psychological Science, 2007

In a randomized trial in middle school classrooms, greeting each student at the door raised academic engaged time by about 20 percent, roughly 12 more minutes on task per class hour, and lowered disruptive behavior.

Cook et al., Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions, 2018

Across 99 studies, warm teacher-student relationships went with higher engagement and achievement, and conflict-filled ones with lower.

Roorda et al., Review of Educational Research, 2011

Slide 1 · Notes

45 minutes. Most students respond to what you already do. Today is about the few who don’t.

Slide 2 · Notes

Volunteers share what they thought was going on, not who. “Every one of those is a guess about why.”

Slide 3 · Notes

Ross Greene’s line. Expectations stay; what changes is how you help a student meet them.

Slide 4 · Notes

Say the second-incident finding plainly and without blame. It’s why slowing down there matters.

Slide 5 · Notes

Learning support leads. Rewrite your card as one skill and one specific problem. “Is defiant” is a label.

Slide 6 · Notes

A flooded student can’t problem solve, and neither can a flooded adult. Safety first, always.

Slide 7 · Notes

Greene’s Plan B. The first step takes longest; most students have never been asked. Pairs practice with their card.

Slide 8 · Notes

Zoe Chance’s line. 2x10 is widely used but lightly tested; it rests on the relationship research.
